journal_name: International Journal of Information Security and Privacy

abstracts.abstract: This paper proposes a novel economic-theoretic framework reconceptualizing privacy decision-making in digital ecosystems, fundamentally shifting from static cost-benefit analyses to dynamic game-theoretic modeling. Traditional privacy calculus models treat information disclosure as a one-time decision, failing to capture the iterative nature of data exchange in interconnected systems. We introduce the Iterative Privacy Equilibrium Framework (IPEF), which models privacy decisions as repeated games among stakeholders with evolving trust relationships and incomplete information. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that equilibrium outcomes in privacy decisions depend critically on network effects, information asymmetries, and temporal discounting factors that existing models neglect. The framework incorporates mechanisms for reputation building, contractual commitment, and strategic information revelation that enable Pareto-superior privacy outcomes. We prove formal results showing that cooperative equilibria are achievable under weaker conditions than previously established in the literature. The contribution extends security economics theory by providing tools to analyze privacy dynamics in platforms where users, service providers, and regulators interact repeatedly. This paradigm shift enables more accurate predictions of privacy behavior and informs the design of incentive-compatible privacy-preserving systems. Managerial implications suggest that organizations can achieve sustainable competitive advantage through transparent privacy practices that build long-term trust capital, challenging conventional wisdom about the short-term costs of privacy investment.

Existing risk management frameworks for information security inadequately address the dynamic nature of contemporary cyber threats, typically treating risk as a static property rather than an evolving phenomenon. This paper presents an Enhanced Dynamic Risk Assessment Model (EDRAM) that significantly improves upon traditional approaches by integrating real-time threat intelligence, behavioral analysis, and adaptive vulnerability scoring. Our theoretical development extends the NIST Risk Management Framework by introducing temporal dimensions and feedback loops that capture the co-evolution of threats and organizational defenses. The model incorporates Bayesian updating mechanisms that refine risk estimates as new intelligence becomes available, addressing a critical gap in static assessment methodologies. We demonstrate through formal analysis that EDRAM produces risk valuations 34% more accurate than conventional approaches when validated against historical incident data from a multi-industry dataset comprising 2,847 security events. The framework introduces novel constructs including threat velocity, defensive resilience quotients, and cascading failure probabilities that provide richer characterization of organizational security posture. Sensitivity analysis reveals that dynamic updating frequency and threat intelligence quality are the primary drivers of assessment accuracy. The theoretical contribution advances risk management scholarship by providing a principled method for incorporating temporal dynamics while maintaining analytical tractability. Practitioners gain actionable guidance for calibrating assessment update frequencies based on their specific threat landscapes and resource constraints.

Centralized identity management systems create single points of failure and force users to cede control of their personal data to third-party authorities, fundamentally misaligning security and privacy incentives. This paper presents DecentID, a novel decentralized identity management architecture that embodies the privacy-by-design principle through the innovative integration of hierarchical deterministic key derivation, zero-knowledge proof circuits, and consent-based selective disclosure mechanisms. Unlike existing self-sovereign identity proposals that focus narrowly on authentication, DecentID provides a comprehensive identity lifecycle management system supporting credential issuance, verification, revocation, and delegation without centralized control. The architecture employs a permissioned distributed ledger with privacy-preserving smart contracts that enforce consent policies while maintaining verifiability. Our system design introduces attribute-based credentials with granular disclosure capabilities, enabling users to prove specific attributes (such as minimum age or professional certification) without revealing underlying identity documents. Security analysis proves forward secrecy, unlinkability across service providers, and resistance to state-level adversaries with quantum computing capabilities. Performance evaluation demonstrates practical applicability with credential issuance completing in 2.3 seconds and verification in 1.1 seconds on commodity hardware. The paradigm shift represented by DecentID challenges the assumption that identity verification requires centralized data accumulation, providing a foundation for privacy-preserving digital interactions across financial services, healthcare, and government applications.

Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) systems face significant scalability and expressiveness challenges when deployed in large-scale enterprise environments with complex organizational structures and dynamic collaboration requirements. This paper presents ScalableABAC, an enhanced access control architecture that substantially improves upon existing ABAC implementations through a novel hybrid policy evaluation engine combining pre-computation caching, parallel processing, and context-aware policy refinement. The system introduces Hierarchical Policy Graphs (HPG) that decompose complex policies into optimized evaluation trees, reducing average authorization latency from O(n) to O(log n) where n represents policy count. Our design addresses the attribute explosion problem through attribute clustering and consolidation techniques that maintain expressiveness while reducing storage requirements by 67% compared to standard implementations. ScalableABAC incorporates machine learning-based anomaly detection that identifies policy conflicts and suggests optimizations, improving policy management efficiency for administrators. The architecture supports hybrid cloud deployments through a federated policy evaluation protocol that maintains consistent security posture across organizational boundaries. Security analysis confirms the system's resistance to attribute inference attacks and policy manipulation. Performance evaluation across simulated enterprise scenarios with up to 10 million concurrent access requests demonstrates 89% latency reduction and 94% throughput improvement over state-of-the-art ABAC systems. The contribution provides organizations with a deployable solution for extending fine-grained access control to high-scale environments while maintaining the flexibility required for dynamic business processes.
